final.title: Maintenance windows are a workflow choice, not a calendar slot
final.body:
If you run a 1–10 person business, rethinking maintenance windows usually comes down to one recurring decision: do you bundle changes into planned downtime, spread them across rolling updates, or use a hybrid? The point is not which sounds cleaner. It is which costs you less in practice: planned customer-visible interruption or unplanned breakdowns.

The useful diagnostic is simple: do you already have a repeatable maintenance workflow? Look for a standard pre-maintenance message, a checklist, a rollback step, and a log of what changed. If those pieces exist, the workflow may be worth tightening. In that case, automation can help with sequencing, reminders, and record-keeping. It should not make the go/no-go call for you. Human approval stays with the owner wherever service might be interrupted or risk increases.

If the process is mostly email, notes, and tool-jumping, the next step is to map the handoffs before automating anything. Otherwise you end up with a neat system wrapped around a messy habit. Nice on paper, not useful in the room.

That is the boundary Bareni looks for: one recurring workflow, one decision owner, one clear outcome. For some businesses, a scoped pilot could cover things like alert consolidation, checklists, or incident reporting. For others, the right answer is to keep it manual for now. If the maintenance work sits inside high-sensitivity, compliance-heavy, or otherwise out-of-scope handling, that is a current scope boundary, not a claim that it can never be automated.
